summary:
Rivers State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, and the Nigerian Criminal Code as applied in the southern states govern conduct there. These sources record no Rivers-specific statute, incident series or enforcement divergence, so the federal rules are what a visitor to Port Harcourt should expect to face.

The 2014 Act reaches far beyond marriage. It renders same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal, criminalises registering, operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations, and bans same-sex cohabitation together with any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) sets the penalty band for the organisational offences at 10 to 14 years' imprisonment and records that police used the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest after it passed.

Sex between men remains criminalised under the Nigerian Criminal Code in the south, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment, and gross indecency carries up to 3 years. Rivers is not one of the twelve northern states where Sharia law operates. The death penalty for male sodomy under state Zina provisions attaches to those northern states, and the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that Sharia criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women there.

One part of the statute has been struck down. In 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists sued over Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act, and the court ruled them unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, which effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise freely. The ruling does not decriminalise same-sex conduct, and Nigeria otherwise offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people.

Enforcement against individuals is documented and extortionate. Human Rights Watch describes arbitrary arrest and police extortion as commonplace after the Act, citing eight of the 21 young men arrested but never charged at a birthday party in Ibadan. The only Port Harcourt-specific incident in these sources is that of Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos who in January 2015 travelled to the city to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook, was attacked and sexually abused there, and did not report it to the police. That case and the nationwide abuse pattern indicate what a same-sex couple or trans visitor faces in Rivers.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Detention raises a further question of placement: press coverage at the sentencing of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that assignment between male and female sections was left to discretion.

Trans-specific violence is on the record. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the national capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. Violence by police against perceived gay people continues as a routine feature of enforcement: in March 2025 Lagos police struck Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped for looking gay, in the mouth with a gun butt and released him only after he paid almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in some northern states, and of the Act's reach to helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.
tangentialFactors:
The national picture is the comparison point for Rivers. Documented incidents cluster in other jurisdictions: a birthday-party mass arrest in Ibadan, a extortion stop by Lagos police, a killing in the national capital. Nothing in these sources shows Rivers enforcing the framework more harshly or more leniently than the rest of Nigeria, and the single Port Harcourt incident is an assault on a visitor rather than a prosecution.

The 2022 constitutional challenge introduced real turbulence into the regime. Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) were ruled unenforceable nationwide, which sits alongside a statute that remains in force for marriage, cohabitation, public displays and same-sex conduct. A visitor reading only the statute, or only the court ruling, would misjudge the position.

External assessments are unusually direct. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice names imprisonment terms, death-penalty exposure and blackmail risk for LGBT+ travellers, and the UK Home Office policy note sets out the secular and religious criminal-law layers separately. Human Rights Watch characterises the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Press handling of trans cases is itself evidence of the environment. Coverage of Bobrisky's April 2024 sentencing foregrounded which prison should hold a crossdresser, and police described the killed transgender woman in Abuja as a man in female clothing.
localsOnly:
Residents live under two overlapping criminal-law layers. The Nigerian Criminal Code applies in the southern states, where sex between men carries up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years, while twelve northern states apply Sharia provisions ranging from lashing to death. Internal movement between the two layers changes the legal exposure for the same conduct.

Since the 2022 ruling, LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals may exist and organise freely, because Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act were declared unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide. Organising remains unprotected in any positive sense: no anti-discrimination, hate-crime or partnership protections exist for LGBTQ+ Nigerians.

Police interaction carries an extortion economy attached to the statute. Human Rights Watch records arbitrary arrest and bribery demands after 2014, and the March 2025 case in Lagos shows a stop for looking gay ending in a 50,000 naira demand and a beating when payment fell short.

Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations against her but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Reporting to police is not a reliable protection route for victims. Daniel did not report his Port Harcourt assault, and six months after the August 2024 killing of the transgender woman in the national capital no suspects had been charged.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted is unresolved in the sources available here; Reuters reports the proposals and the fear they generated in September 2022, but no source confirms their current statutory status.

The scope and practical effect of the 2022 ruling striking Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) is not further sourced: no appeal history, no implementing guidance, and no evidence of how police apply the surviving sections in practice appear in this inventory.

No Rivers State or Port Harcourt enforcement data, prosecution figures, hate-crime records, or local police directives are sourced. The Port Harcourt material consists of one 2015 assault account recorded by Human Rights Watch.

Access to gender-affirming care, identity-document marker changes, restroom and facility rules, and partner or marriage recognition for trans visitors in Rivers are not addressed by any source in this inventory and remain not sourced rather than absent.

The outcome of the August 2024 killing of the transgender woman in the national capital is recorded only up to six months after the event; later developments are not sourced here.
